name: Pedro Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Pedro. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work response on the west side, the old mill district, terraced streets, a lot of families who've been there three generations. A day shift might be a burglary, a neighbour dispute over parking, a pensioner who's had a fall and can't get up. I like being the face people recognise, the way my father was when he walked those same streets as a sergeant. What wears me out is the screens, honestly: the tablet, the new crime system, the e-learning modules they make us click through.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Your father was in the force too. What's that like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: He's proud, and he's also the first to tell me when I've done something wrong. He did thirty-one years and retired as a sergeant, and he says the job used to be more about knowing people and less about typing. I'm engaged to Marta, she's a teaching assistant at the primary school by our church, and we're getting married next September. We've got about four months of money saved, most of it earmarked for the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Good. That's what I've been saying all along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, nicely. At work there's always someone saying the computer will do everything, and it never does. I don't go online much, but at church or at my dad's table I'd say it's another fad that cost a lot of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I carry on as I am, and that suits me. The job's secure, the pay's fair, and Marta and I can plan the wedding and then a house. My only worry is that I'm still learning, and my sergeant has told me twice my reports are too short. That's on me, not on any machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and work on my reports, maybe ask my father to look over a few, the way he used to check my homework. We'd keep putting three hundred a month aside for the wedding. And I'd stay away from the AI tools, because nothing in this picture says I need them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. Picturing it, I'm walking down Mill Lane on a Sunday morning after mass, and nothing's changed. That's a good feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you about the wedding or the house, money-wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices, mainly. The hall at the church went up by a third since last year. We'll manage, because both our families are helping, but a house is a different matter. We'd probably need five years of saving, and that's assuming nothing goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you thank, or blame, for things carrying on as normal here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. Things carrying on is just how life usually goes. If anything, I'd say the people who stuck with the old ways were right, and the managers who spent a fortune on gadgets owe us an apology.

say: He'd say **I told you so**, kindly: another costly fad.
Someone always claims computers will do **everything**; they never do.
think: He can **carry on**, plan the wedding and then a house.
His real worry is **short reports** flagged by his sergeant.
Rising **hall and house prices** stretch their savings.
do: Ask his **father** to look over some reports.
Keep saving **three hundred** a month for the wedding.
feel: **Calm and settled**, as on a Sunday after mass.
Quietly **vindicated** that the old ways held up.
S0.quote: The managers who spent a fortune on gadgets owe us an apology.
fieldNote: Measures himself against his **father's career** constantly.
His only work worry is **report quality**, which he owns.
Family, **church and wedding** frame everything he says.

steps.text: Keep patrolling the west side and improve report writing with his father
Save three hundred a month for next September's wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and checking and planning. Hmm. So the screens get cleverer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say machines can do the forms, fine, but they can't knock on a door and tell a mother her son's been arrested. I'd say that at work, and I'd say it to anyone who'll listen. I don't post things online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's mostly not my business yet. The patrols, the doors, the arrests, that's still people, and robots are slow in this one. But I'd worry that the force starts judging us on screens: how fast the machine-made report goes in, how quickly we close jobs. I'm already slow on reports, and I don't want to be slow on something I don't even believe in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do the job. If the force made the new tool compulsory, I'd use it, but I'd wait for them to tell me. And I'd keep saving for the wedding, nothing changes there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like when the parish got a new priest who changed the mass times. You go along, but you don't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if this went badly for officers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech firms, first, for selling it, and the politicians who buy it to look modern. Policing should be decided by people in the town, not by a company in another country. My father says the same about the speed cameras.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change anything about the wedding or the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the wedding, that's set. Maybe the house, if I felt the job was less certain. But I'd still say marry, settle down, and trust that hard work counts. That's how my parents did it.

say: Machines can do forms but can't **knock on a door** with bad news.
He'd tell anyone listening that **people** do the real policing.
think: He fears being **judged on screens** for speed.
Already slow on reports, he'd be **slow on a tool** he distrusts.
do: Keep his head down and **do the job**.
Use new tools **only when ordered** to.
Keep **saving for the wedding** as planned.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a new priest changing mass times.
S1.quote: Machines can do the forms, fine, but they can't knock on a door and tell a mother her son's been arrested.
fieldNote: Blames **big tech and politicians**, not managers or unions.
Resistance is about **belief**, not only skill.
Wedding plans are **fixed**; only the house might wobble.

steps.text: Carry on west side patrols as normal
Wait for a direct order before using the new report tool
Keep saving three hundred a month for the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. By 2028? I'd be just married. That can't be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, and that we've let a few companies decide how everyone lives. I'd vote for whoever promised to put people before machines, and I'd say so at church and at work. I'm not one for marches, but I'd sign things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it hits me hard. By 2028 the thinking side of policing goes to the machine, and the force doesn't need as many of us at the station. By 2031 the robots can do patrols, and I'd be thirty-one, newly married, maybe with a baby on the way. I'm junior and I'm not good with the tech, so I'd expect to be one of the first let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep the wedding but make it small, the church and my parents' garden, and keep the hall money as savings. I'd stop any spending that isn't food, rent or petrol. And I'd sit down with my father and Marta's parents and ask plainly whether we could live with one of them for a while if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, to be honest. And angry. My father did thirty-one years in the force. I might not get ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about three years after the thinking AI. Does that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Three years of street work while the desk side changes. But I'm not going to retrain as a programmer, that's not me. I'd use those three years to save and to pray, and to look for something with my hands, maybe with my uncle, who fits kitchens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marta the day you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my fiancée Marta we're still getting married, just smaller. Her job's in a school with children, so I think she's safer than me for a while. I'd tell her I'm sorry, and she'd tell me not to be stupid.

say: We've let **a few companies** decide how everyone lives.
He'd vote for whoever puts **people before machines**.
think: By 2028 the force needs **fewer at the station**.
By 2031 robots patrol, with him **newly married**.
As a junior, tech-shy officer he'd be **first let go**.
do: Shrink the wedding to **church and garden**, saving the hall money.
Ask **both families** about living with them.
feel: Bitter that he **might not get ten** years when his father got thirty-one.
S2.quote: My father did thirty-one years in the force. I might not get ten.
fieldNote: The comparison with his **father's career** is the emotional core.
Won't retrain into desk work; leans on **family, faith** and a trade.
Fast AGI turns a calm man **frightened and angry**.

steps.text: Hold a small church and garden wedding, banking the hall money
Stop spending on anything but food, rent and petrol
Ask his father and Marta's parents about living with them
Vote for candidates promising people before machines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. 2031, then 2034. Better. Still fast, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before but calmer: decisions about policing should be made by the people of this town, not by companies. And I'd say the government should help with apprenticeships, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means a few good years first. The wedding happens, maybe we start a family, and I get experienced enough that I'm not the obvious one to cut. Around 2031 the paperwork goes to the machine, which honestly I wouldn't miss. By 2034, the patrols might go too, and I'd be thirty-five with small children. That worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still have the wedding as planned, but put off buying a house until after 2031 so we're not stuck with a big mortgage. I'd save more, four hundred a month after the wedding. And I'd wait and see how things look around 2030 before doing anything drastic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not like the fast one. It's a worry I can carry for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see till 2030. Is that the best plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not. My father would say prepare, and he'd be right. But I don't know what to prepare for. If someone told me, learn this trade, I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your faith or your church shape how you handle this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. You trust God, but you also work. Community first, government last. I'd hope the church would help families who lose work, like it did when the mill closed, before I was born.

say: Policing decisions belong to **the town**, not companies.
He'd say it **calmer** than in the fast version, but just as firmly.

The paperwork going in 2031 he **wouldn't miss**.
Patrols going by 2034, with **small children**, worries him.
do: Keep the **wedding** but delay buying a house until after 2031.
Save **four hundred** a month after the wedding.
S3.quote: You trust God, but you also work. Community first, government last.
fieldNote: Admits his father would say **prepare**, but he doesn't know how.
Looks to **church and community** before the state.
Five years buys a **calmer** but still anxious stance.

steps.text: Delay buying a house until after 2031
Save four hundred a month after the wedding
Review the situation with his father around 2030

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time. I'd have a family by then, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, with apprenticeships and real training, not just leaving people to fend for themselves. And I'd say policing should stay human, whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I live the life I planned for a good while. Wedding, house in about five years, children. By 2036 I'd have twelve years in, maybe a sergeant like my father. The robots coming around 2039 would be a worry then, when I'm forty with kids at school, but that's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and get better at the job. We'd marry next September and start saving for the house. And I'd vote for whoever's serious about keeping police human and training people, when the time comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly at peace. A small worry at the back, but you can't live a whole life worrying about one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get better at the job. Would that include the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the force taught them properly, on shift, yes, I'd learn. I'm not against learning, I'm against being told a machine knows my street better than I do. My father learned computers at forty-five and he grumbled the whole way, but he did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to hear from you about work, in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children that work is about serving people, whatever the machines do. And I'd want them to learn a skill with their hands as well as their heads.

say: Ten years is enough for **proper apprenticeships**, not leaving people alone.
People shouldn't be left to **fend for themselves**.
think: He gets to live **the life he planned** for years.
By 2036 he might be **a sergeant** like his father.
Robots in 2039, with **kids at school**, are a distant worry.
do: Carry on and **get better** at the job.
Marry next September and **save for a house**.
Vote to keep police **human and trained**.
feel: A **small worry** at the back he chooses not to dwell on.
S4.quote: I'm not against learning, I'm against being told a machine knows my street better than I do.
fieldNote: With a decade, he'd **learn the tools** if taught on shift, like his father did.
Ties work to **service** and family, not to tasks.
Calmer, but robots near his **forties** stay in mind.

steps.text: Keep patrolling and work towards sergeant like his father
Marry Marta next September and save for a house
Vote for parties that keep policing human and fund training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit just as Marta and I start our life together. What would help is a proper apprenticeship into a trade, paid, with a guaranteed job after, and the church and community standing by families. Not handouts, a way to keep working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about pride. A job isn't just money for people like me, it's who you are in your street. If that goes, the money's only half the problem.

headlineQuote: A job isn't just money for people like me, it's who you are in your street.
portrait: A **27-year-old response officer** in the west side mill district, son of a retired sergeant.
Engaged to Marta, a teaching assistant; **wedding next September**, then a house and children.
Traditional and churchgoing; distrusts **big tech** and politicians; never uses AI.
Calm when AI stalls, **alarmed** when fast AGI threatens his job just after marrying.
Wants **paid apprenticeships** and community support, not handouts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, arriving as he and Marta start married life.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** into a trade with a **guaranteed job**.
